sentence: Macbeth’s admission that he has no “spur” but “vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” suggests that he recognises the danger of his ambition even as he surrenders to it.
Shakespeare presents unchecked ambition as Macbeth’s hamartia, since it overpowers his conscience even though he concedes that Duncan has been “so clear in his great office”.
Macbeth and Lady Macbeth conspire to murder Duncan beneath their own roof, and the secrecy of their plot is reflected in her instruction to “look like th’innocent flower”.
Lady Macbeth’s advice to “look like th’innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t” reveals a devious mind that treats concealment as a weapon.
The Captain’s gruesome account of Macbeth unseaming Macdonwald “from the nave to th’ chops” presents him as the embodiment of masculinity, equating manliness with violence.
Macbeth begins as a tragic hero, praised as “valour’s minion” for his courage in battle, yet his fatal flaw drives him from admired nobleman to hated outcast.
The witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Cawdor before he knows that Duncan has granted him the title, and this early accuracy tempts him to trust the rest of their prophecy.
The witches’ prophecies create the impression that Macbeth’s fate is fixed, yet his violent choices suggest that he actively shapes the future he claims to fear.
Shakespeare invites the audience to question whether Macbeth acts on free will, since the witches foretell the crown but never instruct him to murder Duncan.
Macbeth’s admission that he is “in blood / Stepped in so far” that retreat would be as tedious as advance makes his downfall seem increasingly inevitable.
The witches’ prophecy that Banquo’s descendants will be kings fuels Macbeth’s insecurity and drives him to murder his friend and attempt to destroy his line.
The witches’ greeting acts as a catalyst, transforming Macbeth’s private ambition into a plan for regicide once Lady Macbeth urges him to act.
Lady Macbeth subverts gender expectations by calling on spirits to “unsex me here”, rejecting the gentle, submissive femininity demanded of a Jacobean woman.
Duncan’s remark that “there’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face” foreshadows the deception Macbeth will practise on the king who trusts him.
After Duncan’s murder, Macbeth maintains a façade of loyal grief, killing the grooms in feigned fury to conceal his own guilt.
Macbeth’s regicide would have horrified a Jacobean audience, who believed in the divine right to rule and regarded the murder of a king as an offence against God.
Macbeth’s acknowledgement that he should “shut the door” against Duncan’s murderer, “not bear the knife” himself, shows his awareness that regicide betrays the duties of hospitality.
Shakespeare uses the soliloquy “Is this a dagger which I see before me?” to expose Macbeth’s inner turmoil as he hesitates on the brink of murder.
Macbeth lists his reasons not to kill Duncan, beginning with the fact that he is the king’s “kinsman and his subject”, yet ambition overrides both loyalty and family bond.
Lady Macbeth seeks to emasculate her husband by insisting that “when you durst do it, then you were a man”, linking courage and murder to manhood.
Lady Macbeth belittles her husband by comparing him to “the poor cat i’ th’ adage”, mocking his reluctance to seize what he desires.
The floating dagger may be a hallucination produced by Macbeth’s guilty imagination, a possibility he voices himself when he calls it “a dagger of the mind, a false creation”.
Through the conjuration of apparitions in Act 4, the witches manipulate Macbeth with reassurances that no man “of woman born” can harm him.
Consumed by guilt after the murder, Macbeth imagines a voice crying “Macbeth shall sleep no more”, suggesting that his conscience has destroyed his peace of mind.
Lady Macbeth attempts to suppress her guilt with the claim that “a little water clears us of this deed”, but her sleepwalking in Act 5 shows that it cannot be washed away.
Shakespeare presents regicide as a violation of the natural order, reflected in the disturbances that follow Duncan’s death, such as an owl killing a falcon and horses eating one another.
The supernatural witches who “look not like th’ inhabitants o’ th’ earth” would have unsettled a Jacobean audience familiar with King James I’s fascination with witchcraft.
Macbeth grows increasingly paranoid, declaring that “to be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus”, since he fears that Banquo’s royal line threatens his throne.
In the exposition, the Captain’s praise of “brave Macbeth” establishes him as a loyal war hero, which makes his later corruption all the more shocking.

In the rising action, Macbeth’s murder of Duncan and his killing of the grooms to conceal it show how one crime demands another, setting him on a path of violence that he will find impossible to abandon.
Fleance’s escape from the murderers in Act 3 is a pivotal moment, because Macbeth’s plan to secure his dynasty fails and his control begins to slip.
In the falling action, Macbeth’s slaughter of Macduff’s family turns the tide against him, as Malcolm declares that “Macbeth / Is ripe for shaking” and an English army prepares to march on Scotland.

In the resolution, Macbeth’s death at the hands of Macduff and Malcolm’s coronation restore order to Scotland, while Macbeth and his queen are dismissed as “this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen”.
Banquo’s ghost is the embodiment of Macbeth’s guilt, a physical manifestation of the murder he ordered that only he is able to see.
Macbeth’s belief in the witches’ words turns their prediction into a self-fulfilling prophecy, since his violent attempts to secure the crown provoke the rebellion that destroys him.
Macbeth’s order to slaughter Macduff’s wife and children confirms his transformation into a tyrant who kills the innocent to calm his own insecurity.
Reflecting the Jacobean belief in the body politic, Duncan’s murder leaves Scotland sick and divided, as Ross laments: “Alas, poor country, / Almost afraid to know itself!”
Lady Macbeth’s psychological unravelling in Act 5, where she sleepwalks and cries “Out, damned spot”, contrasts with her earlier composure and suggests that guilt cannot be suppressed indefinitely.
Macbeth’s hubris peaks when he treats the apparition’s promise as a guarantee of safety, boasting in battle that “I bear a charmed life”.
By Act 5, Macbeth is so desensitised to horror that he admits “I have almost forgot the taste of fears”, showing how violence has hollowed out his conscience.
Macbeth’s response to his wife’s death is nihilistic: he reduces life to “a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing”.
Macbeth experiences anagnorisis when Macduff reveals that he was “from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripped”, and he realises that the witches have deceived him with a double meaning.
Macbeth’s descent into nihilism is complete in the “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow” soliloquy, where time and human life are stripped of all purpose.
Lady Macbeth’s ambition operates within a patriarchal society in which power belongs to men, so she can pursue the crown only by persuading her husband to commit the crime.
The Birlings maintain a façade of respectability at the engagement dinner, but the Inspector’s questioning strips it away to expose their selfishness.
The play offers no neat resolution: although Sheila and Eric accept responsibility, their parents’ refusal to change leaves the moral questions unsettled.
Sheila experiences a form of anagnorisis when she recognises the consequences of her actions and admits, “I know I’m to blame”.
Mr Birling’s dismissal of Eva Smith because “she’d a lot to say — far too much — so she had to go” exposes a complete lack of morality in his business practices.
Priestley’s set is “substantial and heavily comfortable, but not cosy and homelike”, presenting the Birlings’ wealth while hinting at their emotional coldness.
The stage directions change the lighting from “pink and intimate” to “brighter and harder” when the Inspector arrives, symbolising the exposure of the family’s secrets.
Mr Birling views the future through rose-tinted spectacles, confidently insisting that “there isn’t a chance of war” on the eve of the First World War.
Mr Birling’s confident claim that the Titanic is “unsinkable” creates dramatic irony, since Priestley’s 1945 audience knows that it sank on its maiden voyage in 1912.
Mr Birling’s ignorant dismissal of war, declaring that “the Germans don’t want war”, is exposed by the audience’s knowledge of the two world wars that followed.
The Inspector inspects the Birlings’ consciences as closely as their alibis, until their carefully protected reputations begin to crumble.
The Inspector appears omnipotent: he controls the pace of the interrogation, deciding who is questioned and what is revealed, while the family are powerless to resist.
The Inspector seems omniscient, confronting each character with details of their involvement that he should have no way of knowing.
Mr Birling’s belief that “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own” is the creed of capitalism, valuing individual profit above social duty.
Priestley uses the Inspector to promote socialism, insisting that “we are members of one body” in order to urge the audience to value collective responsibility over self-interest.
Mr Birling’s dismissal of striking workers, including Eva Smith, in order to keep wages low demonstrates the exploitation of the working class by capitalists.
An Inspector Calls carries a didactic message: through the Inspector’s final warning of “fire and blood and anguish”, Priestley urges society to accept collective responsibility.
Eva Smith is destroyed by a rigid class system in which a wealthy woman such as Mrs Birling can dismiss a working-class girl as “a girl of that sort”.
Eva Smith is deeply vulnerable: as an unmarried, pregnant, working-class woman with no family to support her, she has nowhere to turn once Mrs Birling’s committee refuses her.
Eva is disempowered at every stage: she loses her job at Birling and Company, then her position at Milwards, and finally the help she seeks from Mrs Birling’s committee.
Gerald Croft’s upper-class background, as the son of Sir George and Lady Croft, makes his engagement to Sheila a social triumph for the ambitious Mr Birling.
The Birlings are middle-class industrialists desperate to rise, which is why Mr Birling is so eager to mention his hopes of a knighthood in the next honours list.
Priestley’s working-class victim never appears on stage, so the audience understands her only through the testimony of the privileged characters who exploited her.
In the play’s moral framework, Mrs Birling’s refusal to help a pregnant girl is a sin, one that the Inspector punishes by leading her to condemn her own son.
An Inspector Calls resembles a morality play: the Inspector acts as a preacher figure who examines each character’s sins before delivering a lesson to the audience.
Mr Birling’s decision to sack Eva Smith shows how the powerful exploit workers, treating labour as a cost to be cut rather than as people to be valued.
Mrs Birling degrades Eva by dismissing her as “a girl of that sort”, using her class prejudice to deny the girl both dignity and help.
Priestley’s progressive message that “we are members of one body” challenges the selfish individualism of the older generation and champions social responsibility.
Mr Birling’s conservative outlook is clear when he dismisses the idea of community as “all that nonsense”, preferring a society in which everyone looks after themselves.
Mrs Birling’s class prejudice blinds her to the truth: she assumes that Eva is lying, and she condemns the father of the child without realising that he is her own son.
Eva Smith suffers discrimination on the grounds of both class and gender, since the Birlings and Gerald hold power over her as a working-class woman with no protection.
Mr Birling’s abuse of power is evident when he dismisses Eva for demanding a modest rise in her wages, protecting his profits at the expense of her livelihood.
The Inspector’s declaration that “each of you helped to kill her” insists that every character is accountable for Eva’s fate, forcing the Birlings to confront their actions.
The final telephone call, announcing that a girl has just died and that a police inspector is on his way, leaves the play on a cliff-hanger that unsettles the audience.
The play’s circular narrative, in which the telephone at the end echoes the Inspector’s ring at the door, suggests that the cycle of responsibility will begin again for anyone who ignores his lesson.
Jekyll maintains a façade of respectability, his reputation as a learned and charitable doctor concealing the “profound duplicity of life” that he later confesses.
Hyde is the embodiment of Jekyll’s repressed desires, a physical form for the impulses that the Victorian gentleman has spent years concealing.
Jekyll’s hubris is evident when he assures Utterson that “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde”, a boast that the rest of the novella disproves.
Jekyll experiences anagnorisis when he wakes to find the hand of Edward Hyde at the end of his own arm, realising too late that he has lost control of the transformation.
Stevenson’s use of third-person limited narration keeps the reader tied to Utterson’s perspective, so the mystery of Hyde’s identity unfolds only as the lawyer investigates.
The narration shifts in the final chapters from Utterson’s limited viewpoint to the first-person accounts of Lanyon and Jekyll, so that the truth is revealed by those who experienced it.
Because events are focalised through Utterson, the reader shares his confusion and curiosity, which builds suspense around the identity of Hyde.
Utterson takes a kind of vicarious pleasure in the wilder lives of his friends, remaining “the last reputable acquaintance” of men who have fallen into disgrace.
Stevenson explores the duality of human nature through Jekyll’s confession that he recognised “the thorough and primitive duality of man”.
Utterson turns to physiognomy, judging Hyde’s character from his “troglodytic” appearance, which reflects the Victorian belief that evil could be read in the face.
Jekyll transgresses the limits of Victorian science and morality when he separates his “polar twins”, seeking to indulge his desires without consequence.
The opening chapters resemble a detective novel, with Utterson vowing “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek” as he sets out to solve the mystery.
Stevenson’s novella is Gothic literature: its fog-bound London, sinister doubles and fear of hidden evil create an atmosphere of dread beneath a respectable surface.
Jekyll’s conclusion that “man is not truly one, but truly two” suggests that evil is inherent in every human being, however respectable they appear.
Utterson’s admission that he follows “Cain’s heresy”, letting his brother “go to the devil in his own way”, reveals a morally passive character who tolerates sin in others.
Mr Guest’s use of graphology, comparing Hyde’s handwriting with Jekyll’s, provides evidence that the two men are connected, since the hands are alike apart from their slope.
Lanyon is traumatised by witnessing Hyde’s transformation into Jekyll, declaring that his “life is shaken to its roots” and that his “days are numbered”.
Hyde’s trampling of the child and murder of Carew display wrath, one of the seven deadly sins, while Jekyll’s refusal to accept any limit on his ambition reflects pride.
Utterson is presented as a man of virtue, drinking “gin when he was alone, to mortify a taste for vintages”, yet Stevenson hints that this restraint comes at the cost of emotional warmth.
Hyde embodies the abject: his “ape-like” fury and “troglodytic” features blur the boundary between man and beast, provoking disgust in everyone who meets him.
Utterson’s fear that he can read “Satan’s signature upon a face” in Hyde’s features gives the villain a satanic quality that would have alarmed devout Victorian readers.
Enfield’s description of Hyde as “some damned Juggernaut” uses hellish imagery, as the word “damned” associates him with Hell while the Juggernaut suggests an unstoppable, crushing force.
Stevenson contrasts the pious respectability of Victorian London, with its churchgoing gentlemen, against the sinful undercurrent that is revealed by Hyde’s crimes.
Jekyll’s experiments border on blasphemy, as he attempts to divide human nature and so usurp a creative power that Victorians believed belonged to God alone.
The novella becomes epistolary in its final chapters, as Lanyon’s letter and Jekyll’s “Full Statement of the Case” replace Utterson’s narration.
Jekyll’s addiction to Hyde grows until the transformations occur involuntarily, and he admits that he is “slowly losing hold of my original and better self”.
Hyde’s “ape-like fury” and Utterson’s description of him as “troglodytic” suggest atavism, reflecting Victorian fears, following Darwin, that humans might regress to a more primitive state.
Walton’s ambition is clear when he declares that “one man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the knowledge which I sought”, an attitude that mirrors Victor’s own recklessness.

The animation of the Creature is the novel’s pivotal moment: Victor’s dream of glory is replaced instantly by “breathless horror and disgust”, and every later tragedy follows from his decision to flee.
The Creature is the embodiment of Victor’s unchecked ambition, a living consequence of his actions that he can neither control nor escape.
Victor transgresses the boundaries of nature when he gathers materials from “the dissecting room and the slaughter-house”, crossing a moral line that Shelley presents as dangerous.
Shelley’s novel is a landmark of Gothic literature, using storms, graveyards and a monstrous creation to explore contemporary fears about the dangers of science.
Victor is traumatised by the sight of his creation, collapsing into “a nervous fever” that confines him for months and leaves him unable to speak of what he has done.
As a product of the Romantic Movement, Frankenstein presents nature as sublime and restorative, as when the Alps briefly calm Victor’s grief, but also as a force that punishes human arrogance.
By creating life, Victor seeks to appropriate divine power, claiming the role of God and bringing destruction on everyone he loves.
Shelley uses a frame narrative, in which Walton’s letters contain Victor’s story and Victor’s story contains the Creature’s, so that the reader must weigh three competing perspectives.
Victor feels entitled to a creator’s glory, imagining that “a new species would bless me as its creator and source” without considering his responsibility for what he makes.
Victor’s sense of superiority is evident when he imagines that “many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me”, casting himself as a benefactor above ordinary humanity.
Victor’s scientific ambition begins with a “bold question” about where “the principle of life” comes from, but Shelley shows how the desire for discovery hardens into obsession.

At the moment of creation Victor holds absolute power over his creature, yet he abandons it immediately, and the later reversal of that power, when the Creature insists “I am your master”, is a direct result.
Victor attempts to displace God as the source of life, a transgression that Shelley punishes by stripping him of his family, his friends and his peace of mind.
Society marginalises the Creature, forcing him to the edges of human settlement, to hovels, forests and glaciers, simply because of his appearance.
Isolation haunts both Walton and Victor: Walton laments “I have no friend, Margaret”, while Victor’s secrecy cuts him off from the family who might have helped him.
The Creature’s sense of self is shaped by what he reads: Paradise Lost makes him question whether he resembles Adam, the first man, or Satan, the outcast.
Victor dehumanises the Creature by calling him a “wretch” and a “monster”, refusing him the sympathy due to a thinking and feeling being.
Frankenstein reflects the Enlightenment faith in reason and scientific progress, while warning that knowledge pursued without moral responsibility can destroy those who seek it.
As a cautionary tale, the novel warns readers of the dangers of unrestrained ambition, as Victor’s pursuit of knowledge destroys William, Justine, Clerval and Elizabeth.
Shelley’s imagery of fire and lightning, such as the oak shattered by a bolt in Chapter 2, foreshadows the destructive power of the science that Victor will later unleash.
Walton and Victor each describe their ambitions as an enterprise of glory, yet Shelley shows that both are willing to risk human lives for it.
The desolation of the Arctic setting, an empty landscape of ice, reflects the emotional emptiness of Walton and Victor, who have chosen ambition over companionship.
Victor’s retreat into the solitudes of his laboratory cuts him off from family and friends, and Shelley suggests that this isolation allows his obsession to grow unchecked.
Walton declares that he will “satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited”, language that presents exploration as an appetite that must be fed.
Victor’s laborious experiments, “days and nights of incredible labour and fatigue”, show how single-mindedly he pursues forbidden knowledge.
In his grief Victor is “encompassed by a cloud which no beneficial influence could penetrate”, an image that suggests how guilt has cut him off from comfort and hope.
Victor is assailed by guilt after William’s murder, unable to confess because he fears that no one would believe his story.
Walton admits that he bitterly feels “the want of a friend”, revealing a loneliness that parallels Victor’s.
When Walton first sees him, Victor is “dreadfully emaciated by fatigue and suffering”, a physical sign of the cost of his obsession.
Fatigue and fear grip Walton’s crew as the ship is trapped in the ice, adding pressure to the question of whether ambition should outweigh the lives of the men.
Victor’s study of the human body, from the blooming cheek of life to the decaying frame of the dead, leads him to the dangerous idea that he can reverse death.
The rambles that Victor takes with Henry Clerval restore some of his health and happiness, contrasting with the solitary labour that has destroyed his peace.
Victor’s inexhaustible appetite for knowledge sets him apart from Clerval, whose interests in language, people and moral life are more human.
Victor’s childhood is full of parental caresses and affection, which makes the Creature’s total lack of such care all the more shocking.
The Creature insists that he was once benevolent, declaring “I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend”, and so blames his rejection for his later violence.
Victor makes knowledge an idol, worshipping the pursuit of discovery at the expense of his family and his own wellbeing.
Walton’s fervent desire to reach the North Pole is expressed in his “ardent curiosity”, which parallels Victor’s own obsessive drive for discovery.
The Creature’s longing for a companion who will not flee from him drives his demand that Victor make a female partner.
Not even the beauty of the Alps can fully penetrate Victor’s guilt, since his grief returns even in the sublime landscape of Chamonix.
The Creature’s strength and resistance to cold make him seem invulnerable, which explains why Victor’s pursuit across the Arctic ends in failure.
Victor presents himself as a pioneer of science whose discoveries will benefit humankind, yet he fails to consider the responsibilities that his creation will bring.
Victor’s research draws him to graveyards and charnel-houses, where he studies decay in order to understand life, a grim setting that Shelley uses to signal the unnatural nature of his work.
Victor inherited his fascination with alchemy from the writings of Cornelius Agrippa, which his father dismisses as “sad trash”, a warning that Victor ignores.
Victor admits that he disturbed “the tremendous secrets of the human frame” with “profane fingers”, language that presents his research as sacrilege against nature and God.
Victor remains insensible to the Creature’s suffering, seeing only a monster rather than a being that has been abandoned by its maker.
The novel suggests that science which challenges the immutable laws of nature leads to disaster, as Victor’s experiment brings death to those he loves.
The serene beauty of the Swiss landscape offers Victor a brief respite from his guilt, but Shelley shows that nature’s calm cannot repair the damage caused by his ambition.
The Creature’s ecstasy at the beauty of spring and the sound of the cottagers’ music is a rare moment of joy that makes his later rejection even more painful.
In Victor’s nightmare, Elizabeth’s lips become “livid with the hue of death” as he kisses her, a premonition of her murder and a symbol of the death that his creation brings.

The miniature portrait of Victor’s mother, planted on Justine, becomes the false evidence that condemns her, showing how the Creature’s malice and Victor’s silence combine to destroy an innocent life.
The Creature repeatedly seems to elude all pursuit, vanishing into mountains and ice, which reinforces his inhuman strength and Victor’s helplessness.
Victor’s aim to “infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing” suggests a god-like power, though the result is horror rather than glory.
Victor’s horror at the “convulsive motion” that agitates the Creature’s limbs shows how quickly his dream turns into a nightmare.
Victor describes the Creature’s “lustrous black” hair and “pearly” teeth, but these features only create a horrid contrast with his watery eyes and yellow skin.
The Creature’s first sounds are inarticulate, but he soon learns language from the De Laceys, and his eloquent narration overturns Victor’s view that he is a mindless monster.
Victor’s horror at the “demoniacal corpse” to which he has given life shows that his disgust is directed at the Creature’s appearance, not at any evil in his nature.
Walton’s first sight of Victor is of a man in so “wretched a condition” that it provokes pity, preparing the reader for his tragic story.
The Creature is grievously hurt, physically and emotionally, when Felix strikes him with a stick and drives him from the cottage that he had come to regard as home.
The Creature takes refuge in a hovel beside the De Laceys’ cottage, from where he learns about human kindness while remaining excluded from it.
From the shelter of his hovel, the Creature observes the De Laceys’ affection for one another, an experience that teaches him what he has been denied.
The Creature watches the cottagers through the “innumerable chinks” of his hovel, an image that places him literally on the outside of human society, peering in.
The villagers’ violent attack on the Creature, who has just saved a girl from drowning, exposes the barbarity of a society that judges by appearance alone.
The Creature’s wish to be virtuous is shown when he secretly gathers firewood for the De Laceys, which suggests that his later violence is the result of rejection rather than nature.
Shelley presents the violent responses of the villagers and of Felix as base, because their cruelty is provoked by nothing more than the Creature’s appearance.
Rejected by everyone he meets, the Creature comes to see himself as a blot on the world, a victim of prejudice rather than the origin of evil.
Because Victor treats his creation as a blot upon the earth, something to be hidden and forgotten, the Creature is left to learn about humanity alone.
Victor has disowned his creation, refusing to take any responsibility for the life that he gave.
Victor’s repeated use of the word “wretch” reduces the Creature to an object of disgust, the very prejudice that drives the Creature’s rage.
Victor proves irresolute when he first hesitates over making a female creature and then destroys her, leaving the Creature’s plea for a companion unanswered.
The Creature is deserted by his maker the moment he is brought to life, a rejection that Shelley presents as the origin of all the suffering that follows.
Shelley presents Justine as an amiable and devoted servant, which makes her conviction for William’s murder all the more tragic.
Victor’s despair after Elizabeth’s murder turns grief into an obsessive hunt for the Creature across the Arctic, a quest that finally costs him his life.
The Creature secretly acts as a benefactor to the De Laceys, gathering firewood for them while they remain unaware of him, which shows his capacity for kindness.
The cottagers’ consternation when they see the Creature, as Agatha faints and Felix attacks him, shows how appearance overrides everything that he has done for them.
The Creature’s benevolence towards the De Laceys is repaid with violence, a betrayal that begins his transformation from gentle observer into vengeful outcast.
Victor’s pursuit of vengeance after Elizabeth’s death mirrors the Creature’s own thirst for revenge, blurring the line between creator and creation.
The Creature approaches the blind De Lacey because he hopes that an old man who cannot see him will be unprejudiced and will judge him by his words alone.
The Creature imbibed language and moral ideas from the De Laceys and from books such as Paradise Lost, which shows that he has learned to think and feel like a human being.
The Creature’s desolate existence in the wilderness, hunted and alone, is the direct result of Victor’s failure to care for him.
William’s scream that the Creature is an “ogre” who will “eat” him shows how childish fears and fairytale expectations shape reactions to the Creature’s appearance.
Victor loads the Creature with epithets such as “abhorred monster” and “fiend”, rejecting him before he has had a chance to speak.
The Creature’s deepest need is for an interchange of sympathies with the cottagers, a mutual kindness that his appearance makes impossible.
However kind the Creature’s actions, his appearance creates insurmountable barriers between himself and the De Laceys, showing how prejudice defeats even good intentions.
The Creature rejects any submission of abject slavery, and by the time he commands Victor to “obey”, the balance of power between creator and creation has reversed.
After Victor destroys the female creature, the Creature’s rage becomes inextinguishable, and he vows, “I shall be with you on your wedding-night”.
The Creature studies the cottagers’ countenances to understand human feeling, an irony given that it is his own countenance that causes them to reject him.
The Creature’s plea that he ought to be Victor’s Adam is a supplication addressed to his creator as to a god, which makes Victor’s refusal feel like abandonment by heaven itself.
Victor describes the Creature as an “abhorred monster”, language that reveals his own prejudice more than any evil in the being he made.
The Creature’s statement that he considers Satan “the fitter emblem of my condition” shows how his reading of Paradise Lost shapes his view of himself as an outcast.
Justine’s execution is a miscarriage of justice, since she is convicted on circumstantial evidence and a confession extracted under pressure from her priest.
Shelley uses Justine’s trial to criticise the justice system, which convicts an innocent servant on circumstantial evidence while the real culprit goes free.
Justine’s trial shows that justice in Geneva depends on appearances rather than the truth, a failure that Victor’s silence makes even worse.
Victor’s silence while Justine is condemned is the novel’s clearest injustice, since he knows that the Creature, not Justine, killed William.
Shelley presents the verdict against Justine as unjust, since it rests on the miniature found in her pocket and on a confession pressed from her by her priest.
A just court would have weighed the evidence fairly, yet Geneva condemns Justine because the miniature in her pocket looks damning.
The Creature’s humanity is clearest in his longing for companionship and his kindness to the De Laceys, which contrasts with the cruelty of those who reject him.
In ‘Bayonet Charge’, the soldier is consumed by fear and instinct, running “raw / In raw-seamed hot khaki” with no time to think about why he is fighting.
In ‘Ozymandias’, the “sneer of cold command” on the ruined face suggests a tyrant whose power rested on fear, an arrogance that Shelley reduces to rubble.
Ozymandias’s hubris is captured by his boast, “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!”, which Shelley undercuts by showing only “lone and level sands” where his empire once stood.
‘My Last Duchess’ exposes a patriarchal society in which the Duke treats his wife as a possession, controlling and finally silencing her when her behaviour does not meet his expectations.
In ‘The Prelude’, the mountain appears omnipotent as it “towered up between me and the stars”, dwarfing the speaker and making human power seem insignificant.
The Duchess is disempowered by her husband, who admits “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together”, a chilling euphemism for her silencing.
The charge is futile, since the six hundred ride into “the valley of Death” because “someone had blundered”, yet Tennyson still praises their obedience.
Tennyson’s repetition of “Cannon to right of them, / Cannon to left of them” presents the soldiers as cannon-fodder, surrounded by enemy fire with no hope of survival.
Tennyson’s galloping rhythm and repeated phrases give the poem the quality of a ballad, a form traditionally used to commemorate heroic deeds and to shape how a battle is remembered.
Hughes suggests that the soldier is disillusioned, as ideals such as “King, honour, human dignity, etcetera” are “dropped like luxuries” once the reality of battle begins.

The speaker of ‘Remains’ shows the symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder, as the memory of the looter’s death returns long after he has left the army: “he’s here in my head when I close my eyes”.

The soldier’s early idealism seems delusional once the reality of the battlefield replaces his “patriotic tear” with sweat and terror, since nothing he was told prepared him for the violence he now faces.
Hughes presents patriotism as an empty abstraction: the soldier’s “patriotic tear” turns into “molten iron”, suggesting that love of country cannot survive the terror of combat.
Hughes questions the nationalism that drives countries to war by asking what “cold clockwork of the stars and the nations” has turned an ordinary man into a part of a mechanism.
The pilot in ‘Kamikaze’ is treated as disposable, sent off with “enough fuel for a one-way journey / into history”, his individual life valued less than the cause he serves.
The pilot has been indoctrinated by a militaristic culture, as the “powerful incantations” in his “shaven head” suggest an almost religious obedience.

The volta in ‘Ozymandias’ comes at “And on the pedestal, these words appear”, shifting the poem from a description of the ruined statue to the king’s boast, so that his arrogance is immediately undercut by the ruin.
In ‘The Prelude’, Wordsworth presents the sublime when the huge black peak rises behind the rowing boat, a power so overwhelming that it fills the speaker with both awe and terror.
Wordsworth, a poet of the Romantic Movement, presents nature as a powerful force that humbles human arrogance, as the mountain in ‘The Prelude’ towers over the speaker.
‘The Prelude’ is an extract from an epic poem about the growth of Wordsworth’s own mind, which gives an ordinary night on a boat the grandeur of a heroic journey.
Armitage gives a voice to the war veteran in ‘Remains’, showing that the soldier’s traumatic memory continues long after he has left the battlefield.
In ‘War Photographer’, Duffy’s photojournalist develops his films in a darkroom “as though this were a church”, suggesting that his work is a form of sacred witness.
The newspaper readers are complicit in the suffering, Duffy implies, as their eyeballs prick with tears “between the bath and pre-lunch beers” before they return to their comfortable lives.
Duffy criticises public apathy by showing the readers’ brief sympathy dissolving as they turn the page, ending with the blunt verdict that “they do not care”.
Weir presents the mother’s grief through physical imagery, with the poppy’s “spasms of paper red” suggesting that her sorrow is a constant, bodily pain.

Dharker conveys the fragility of human life and its structures through the image of paper “that lets the light / shine through”, suggesting that even the documents that govern our lives are thin and temporary.
The poem’s focus on thin, light-filled paper emphasises transience, since the borders drawn on maps and the monuments of cities are as temporary as the pages themselves.
Blake presents the oppression of London’s poor through the “mind-forg’d manacles” that bind every citizen, suggesting that people are trapped as much by their own acceptance as by their rulers.
Agard explores the lasting effect of colonisation on Caribbean identity, showing how a British education taught him about “Dick Whittington and he cat” while hiding the history of his own people.
The soldier in ‘Poppies’ is one of the direct victims of war, but Weir shifts attention from his death to the mother who must live with its consequences.
The mother in ‘Poppies’ is one of the indirect victims of war: although she never fights, she is left to grieve in a home that has fallen silent without her son.
Armitage conveys trauma through the speaker’s intrusive memories, as the looter’s death replays in his mind: “his bloody life in my bloody hands”.

In ‘Remains’, the soldier’s guilt is suggested by the repetition of “bloody” and by his attempt to excuse himself with “Probably armed, possibly not”, a phrase that fails to remove his sense of responsibility.
Many of the poems present conflict not only as battle but as an internal struggle, as when the speaker of ‘Remains’ must fight the memories that return to him after the war has ended.
In ‘Ozymandias’, Shelley shows that political power is temporary: the “colossal Wreck” stands as a reminder that even the greatest rulers are eventually erased by time.
Agard presents identity as something that must be reclaimed, ending with “I carving out me identity” to show that he is shaping a self from the history he was denied.
In ‘The Emigree’, Rumens shows how memory preserves a city in perfect sunlight, even though the speaker knows that the real place has changed: “I am branded by an impression of sunlight”.
‘Poppies’ and ‘Remains’ show the indirect effects of war: a mother’s grief at home and a veteran’s trauma years later, both of which continue long after the fighting has stopped.
Romanticism’s belief in the power of nature is clear when the mountain in ‘The Prelude’ makes the speaker feel small, as “huge and mighty forms” trouble his thoughts for days afterwards.
Macbeth’s regicide breaks the great chain of being, because Duncan, as king, stands directly beneath God.
